title: Aurora Story: Tracing an Aurora From Solar Storm to Colored Sky
tagline: An interactive D3 story that follows an aurora from solar storm to colored sky.
summary: A Data Visualization class project: an interactive scrollytelling page that follows an aurora from the Sun's solar wind, through Earth's magnetic field and storm indicators, to the colors it paints at different altitudes.
bullets: Told the story in five chapters, from solar wind reaching Earth to auroras over time, built around the May 2024 geomagnetic storm.
Visualized NOAA space weather data with D3, including solar wind clusters by plasma density and temperature, magnetic field (Bz) direction, and the Kp index across stations and time.
Built an interactive atmosphere panel that scrolls through the aurora to show why its colors change with altitude.
Team project with Sudarsna Mukund, Fletcher Gornick and Sam Chea.

title: SourceLens: LLM-Based Assistant for Paper Reading
tagline: An LLM-powered reading canvas that brings papers, citations and evidence together.
summary: A CSCI 8615 project that unifies paper reading, citation exploration, and LLM evidence in a single interactive canvas.
bullets: Designed the full interface layout and interaction flow through iterative sketches and UI prototypes.
Conducted user research by observing a participant using the app and identifying usability improvements for a more intuitive experience.
Built the keyword filter feature, enabling users to click a keyword and instantly surface all references containing it.
Implemented the favorites system for saving papers users want to revisit later.
Created the overview panel, allowing users to quickly browse all paper sections and jump directly to any chapter.

title: JugglAR: Mixed Reality for Task Learning & Muscle Memory
tagline: A hand-tracked AR juggling trainer, and a user study testing whether the skill carries over to real balls.
summary: JugglAR is a hand-tracked augmented reality app for the Meta Quest 3 that lets beginners practice juggling with virtual balls whose speed and gravity can be adjusted. We ran a two-week study comparing people who learned with JugglAR against people who practiced only with real balls, to see whether muscle memory built in AR transfers to the physical task.
bullets: Designed user study and instrumentation.
Explored slowed-down virtual trajectories for motor learning.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Learning to juggle is frustrating at first. Beginners spend much of their practice time picking up dropped balls, and the pace makes it hard to follow three balls at once. Earlier systems either added visual feedback to a single real ball (Juggling 4.0) or trained in VR with handheld controllers (Juggling in VR), so neither practiced the real catching and throwing motions.
We wanted to find out whether practicing with your own hands in AR, at a slower and adjustable pace, builds muscle memory that carries over to real juggling.

sections.heading: What we built
bullets: Built in Unity for the Meta Quest 3, using AR passthrough instead of full VR: early testing showed full immersion was more distracting for learning to juggle.
Catches use recorded hand poses and a closed-fist grip instead of the usual AR pinch gesture, so practice builds the same motion as catching a real ball.
A pinch grab is used only to hold the third ball for the first throw, which solves the hand tracker's trouble with two balls in one hand.
Ball speed and gravity can be adjusted, so learners can slow the pattern down while they learn it.
After a two-hour formative study, we added a tennis-ball catch sound to confirm catches outside the headset's narrow field of view, and improved tracking with more recorded and hand-modeled poses.

sections.heading: The study
paragraphs: Eight people aged 23 to 29 with no juggling experience were split into an AR group and a physical-practice group. Both groups had four sessions over two weeks: a 30-minute first session with a 10-minute tutorial video, then three 20-minute practice sessions. The AR group alternated between JugglAR and real balls.

The goal was to complete a full three-ball juggling cycle on two separate occasions, which requires every ball to pass through both hands. We recorded the session and the exact time at which each participant reached it.

sections.heading: What we found
paragraphs: All four AR participants learned to juggle real balls within three sessions, two of them during the very first session. In the physical group, two participants reached the goal, one regressed in the final session, and one felt overwhelmed and lost the motivation to continue.

AR participants said the app helped them understand the mechanics of juggling and build confidence. The main drawbacks were the headset's limited field of view, especially when looking up or catching with a hand out of view, and the lack of the feeling of catching a ball. With only eight participants, the results are promising rather than conclusive.

sections.heading: Next steps
bullets: Haptic gloves to simulate the feel of a catch.
More control over speed, gravity and the number of balls, and a gamified version to test whether it improves motivation.
A follow-up study comparing AR-only training followed by real balls against switching between the two throughout.
